newsitem.title: UK: Irish hoteliers welcome IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Irish hoteliers welcome IRA ceasefire.

text.p: Northern Ireland hoteliers, worried about a decline in tourism because of guerrilla violence, hailed Saturday's IRA ceasefire as a "positive announcement" for their beleagured industry.

"The impact of the tarnished image of Northern Ireland on potential visitors is well documented and it is recognised that the tourist industry is the first to suffer," the Hositality Association of Northern Ireland said in a statement.

The association said that it had already begun working to attract more visitors after Saturday's announcement by the Irish Republican Army of a new ceasefire to its war against British rule of Northern Irland.
It said that a permanent end to violence and the start of talks were "the essential first steps in the search for long-term peace and stability in our community."

"As our image improves, we in the tourist industry, are committed to actively promoting Northern Ireland across the world as a holiday destination and thus playing our part in growing our economy and providing more employment," it said.

Last week tourism officials reported holiday cancellations after days of rioting by Catholic youths over the routing of Protestant parades through Catholic areas. Industry officials said that coach operators cancelled at least two visits to the British province and more cancellations were expected in the wake of the worst violence Northern Ireland has suffered in years.

They voiced fears that Northern Ireland's image would be for ever linked to violence and said the industry might take years to recover from a high point it reached in 1995 after the IRA's first, 17-month ceasefire.
Northern Ireland's business community saw tourism as a key to job-creation and economic growth and launched an unprecedented marketing campaign after the IRA called a ceasefire in August 1994.
Holiday tourism surged by 67 per cent after that ceasefire but dropped by 20 per cent last year when the guerrillas ended their truce and went back to war.

The ceasefire and 17 months of peace that followed raised hopes in the industry and government that tourism could grow from contributing two percent of gross domestic product to the six percent enjoyed by neighbouring Ireland and Scotland.
More than 1.5 million people, equivalent to the province's entire population, came to the province in 1995, prompting a surge in hotel-building.
But the number of tourists dropped by 20 per cent in 1996 after the ceasefire collapsed.
Tourism employs 13,000 people directly plus another 20,000 in allied sectors such as catering and transport.
But industry officials say it should be employing 20,000 people directly and contributing 500 million pounds ($850 million) to the economy.
